summaries.example: Imagine a science team studying a star. People may see a bright dot in the sky, but scientists also use rules and calculations to describe its motion. Natorp thought philosophy should ask how those rules make scientific knowledge possible. The answer is not just what one person sees; it is a careful method that others can check.
summaries.summary: Paul Natorp was a German philosopher connected with the Marburg School of neo-Kantianism. He wanted philosophy to be as careful as science, but he did not think philosophy should compete with science by inventing a separate picture of reality. Instead, philosophy should examine the rules and methods that make scientific knowledge possible. Natorp called this kind of work a transcendental method. He said science is always developing: thinkers make hypotheses, test and revise ways of organizing experience, and move toward more complete knowledge without reaching a final answer. He also argued that thinking actively organizes what we know. In his view, objects studied by science are not simply handed to the mind ready-made; they become clear through concepts, laws, and methods. Natorp’s psychology tried to understand personal experience indirectly by moving backward from the objective ideas people form. His history of philosophy connected the growth of science with moments when thinkers became aware of how their methods worked. His interpretation of Plato treated Plato’s ideas as guiding principles for thought, rather than as separate magical things.
key_ideas: Natorp belonged to the Marburg School, a group of thinkers who looked to Kant for a careful task for philosophy.
He thought philosophy should study how science becomes objective, or shareable and checkable by different thinkers.
Science is not a finished building. It is an ongoing activity that improves through methods and hypotheses.
Natorp also studied psychology and the history of philosophy, especially Plato, to understand how thinking develops.
summaries.why_it_matters: Natorp’s work encourages us to ask not only whether a claim is true, but also how a claim becomes clear, testable, and useful to many people. It connects science, thinking, psychology, and the history of ideas. His approach also shows that knowledge can be reliable while still remaining open to improvement.

important_terms.definition: A way of asking what must be true or in place for knowledge to be possible and justified.
An idea or rule proposed to help organize experience and guide further investigation. It can be improved or replaced.
A careful study of the rules that help thinking make knowledge and objects clear.
The view that we should study knowledge, science, and culture critically instead of making guesses beyond experience.

summaries.example: Consider the scientific concept of gravity. A student may experience an object falling, while physics formulates equations that describe and predict motion. For Natorp, philosophy should not mainly ask about a hidden object beyond all possible knowledge. It should examine how concepts, mathematical relations, and laws transform appearances into an objective scientific phenomenon. Because every formulation remains open to more exact determination, science is an ongoing task rather than a completed system.
summaries.summary: Paul Natorp was a major figure in Marburg neo-Kantianism, a movement that returned to Kant not by simply repeating Kant’s doctrines, but by trying to philosophize in a critical and scientifically responsible spirit. Natorp’s central tool was the transcendental method. Starting from successful forms of knowledge—especially mathematical natural science—philosophy asks what conditions make their objectivity and justification possible. It therefore avoids speculative claims about a reality wholly beyond experience while also refusing to reduce knowledge to private psychology. This anti-psychologism is central: logical validity cannot depend on the changing states of an individual mind. Natorp’s philosophy of science describes science as a fieri, an ongoing process rather than a finished fact. Its progress is methodical because it proceeds through hypotheses, understood actively as conceptual acts that establish a lawful basis for interpreting phenomena. Scientific objects such as planets or physical forces are not merely sensory givens; they are progressively determined through concepts, mathematical structures, and laws. Natorp’s genetic logic reconstructs the synthetic operations by which thinking forms such objects. He thus gives philosophy a reflective role: science formulates laws, while philosophy examines the more general principles of that law-governed activity. Natorp’s critical psychology complements this project. Since immediate subjective experience cannot itself become an objective object without being transformed, psychology must approach subjectivity indirectly by regressing from its objectivations. key_ideas: Natorp’s Marburg neo-Kantianism treats philosophy as a critique of science: it explains the conditions of objectivity rather than producing an independent speculative science.
He rejects psychologism because reducing logic and truth to individual mental processes would undermine their universal validity.
Scientific knowledge is dynamic. Its objectivity lies in regulated method and lawfulness, not in a permanent set of unchangeable scientific principles.
Natorp interprets hypotheses as active acts of positing or grounding. Scientific objects are progressively formed through concepts, laws, and calculations.
His account distinguishes subjective appearance from the objective, scientifically determinable phenomenon constructed through lawful thinking.

His history of philosophy joins systematic analysis with historical development, and his reading of Plato treats the Forms as critical or categorial principles rather than separately existing entities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Natorp offers a demanding account of objectivity that does not depend on treating knowledge as a mirror of ready-made things or as a report of private experiences. His view helps explain why scientific concepts can be constructed, revisable, and historically changing while still being governed by standards that are meant to hold for any thinker. It also illustrates a broader philosophical question: should philosophy discover new facts, or should it clarify the conditions and ideals that make knowledge possible? His work connects that question to logic, psychology, Plato, and the development of science.

important_terms.definition: A Kant-inspired procedure that begins with an established form of knowledge and asks what principles justify or make it possible.
Natorp’s term for the active establishment of a law or conceptual basis that allows experience to become scientifically intelligible.
A philosophy of science concerned with the lawful activity by which thinking constructs progressively determinate objects of knowledge.
The doctrine that objective knowledge should not be grounded in contingent psychological states or private mental events.
An ideal boundary or goal of inquiry: complete determination of an object, which finite thinkers can approach but never finally reach.
A methodical reconstruction of earlier, less objective stages of experience by working backward from already formed objects of knowledge.
The philosophical position that examines the conditions of rational knowledge and culture while rejecting speculative claims beyond experience.

questions_to_think_about: If scientific concepts are constructed by thought, in what sense can science still be objective?
Why would grounding logic in psychology threaten the idea of universal truth?
Does an unreachable ideal of complete knowledge guide inquiry effectively, or make knowledge seem permanently incomplete?
What is gained, and what might be lost, by interpreting Plato through a modern theory of scientific method?

summaries.example: Suppose your class builds a model of a solar system. At first, you may use a simple rule: planets move in circles. Later, better observations lead you to use a more accurate rule. Natorp would say that science grows through this kind of organized improvement. Philosophy asks what makes the rules count as knowledge and why a method can be checked by everyone, not just by the person who invented it.
summaries.summary: Paul Natorp was a German philosopher associated with the Marburg School, a branch of neo-Kantianism. The Marburg thinkers believed Kant could help philosophy recover a serious task after the decline of large speculative systems. They did not simply copy Kant. They focused on the transcendental method: beginning with successful knowledge, especially mathematical science, and asking what makes it possible and justified. Natorp thought philosophy should protect rational inquiry from two dangers. One was speculation that claims to know what lies beyond experience. The other was psychologism, the attempt to explain logic and truth only through a person’s mental events. If truth were just a report about someone’s mind, it would lose its universal character. Natorp described science as an activity that develops over time. Scientists do not start with a final collection of fixed principles. They use hypotheses—active proposals that organize experience and establish a basis for further investigation. A scientific object, such as a planet, is therefore not simply a sensory picture. It is made objectively understandable through concepts, measurements, mathematical relations, and laws. Thinking is a kind of activity or function that unifies what would otherwise be unclear or scattered. Logic studies the general rules of this object-forming activity, while science applies more specific laws in its investigations. Natorp’s critical psychology approaches immediate subjectivity indirectly. It studies the earlier, less objective stages that can be reconstructed from the ideas and objects already formed in science. key_ideas: Natorp was part of the Marburg School, which developed a modern form of Kant-inspired philosophy.
He believed philosophy should study science’s conditions of objectivity instead of making unsupported guesses about a world beyond experience.
For Natorp, science is an active process that keeps changing through methods and hypotheses.
He thought thinking does not merely receive finished objects; it organizes and determines them through concepts and laws.
His psychology and history of philosophy extend the same question: how does thinking become clear about its own activity?
His interpretation of Plato connected Plato’s ideas with guiding principles for thought, not with separate objects hidden somewhere else.
summaries.why_it_matters: Natorp matters because he presents knowledge as both objective and unfinished. Scientific ideas can be made through human thinking without becoming mere personal opinions, because they are organized by methods and laws intended to be shareable and rationally checkable. His work also shows how one philosophical approach can connect questions about science, logic, psychology, and the history of ideas.

important_terms.definition: A method that asks what conditions make knowledge possible, reliable, and open to justification.
A proposed rule or idea used to organize evidence and guide further work; it may be revised as inquiry continues.
The study of how thinking is organized, especially how it forms concepts, rules, and connected knowledge.
The idea that truth and logic should not depend only on what happens inside one person’s mind.
An ideal goal that guides inquiry even though people may never fully reach it.
Natorp’s attempt to study subjectivity indirectly by working backward from the objective ideas people create.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a philosopher study the rules behind science instead of trying to do the same experiments as scientists?
Can knowledge be objective if it is shaped by human concepts?
Why could changing a scientific theory be a sign of progress rather than failure?
How might the history of science help us understand what science is?
